Designer, businessman and DJ(?) THEE multi-hyphenate Sabyasachi Mukherji (whose nickname is Pepsi btw) takes on the most unsparing group of people at his Delhi store launch— fashion journalists. All ready with their phone cameras, hungry (actually greedy even after a generous lunch) for a “byte”, cornering the designer in his jewellery room. With the double whammy of extreme wit lathered with his humour, Sabya answers all their loaded questions. Like— what kind of clothes he wants to make, why hand-work will trump AI and how bad journalism is comparable to fast food? 🤪 

The last time he spoke to the press was almost two years ago, making this a moment rarer than a solar eclipse: Sabya, candid and unfiltered. Enjoy.

Iconic Fashion Director Nicola Formichetti is hardly new to the theatre of Indianwear. Remember the three-piece TT bikini sari he put Gaga in during her 2010 LAP visit? Delhi gays will remember the lore. 

He has one of fashion’s more ludicrously extensive CVs, designer, editor, stylist, et al., but as Creative Director at M·A·C, he now comes head-on with perhaps fashion’s most formidable final boss: the Big Fat Indian Wedding.

For the new campaign, Nicola assembles the entire shaadi cinematic universe: the bride, the mother of the bride, the cousin, the bridesmaid who looks suspiciously ready to upstage everyone the minute “Bole Chudiyan” comes on. It’s essentially an editorial GRWM crossed with one giant family portrait, zooming in on the bit wedding advertising rarely bothers with but everyone secretly fantasises about: the getting ready of it all. The room full of lehengas, jewellery, opinions, someone asking where the safety pins are, an auntie doing quality control, and an entire glam battalion spraying, baking and blending that foundation into matrimonial permanence before someone cues the planned slo-mo 🤪👀

And conspicuously, there is no groom in the picture. Cute. Perhaps the real target demographic are the girlies who desperately want the wedding but have absolutely no interest in the marriage. I stan, baby. I stan!

The diaphanous chiffon saris, the pearls, those now-iconic photographs with Jackie Kennedy: practically fashion’s holy scripture. But let’s not reduce a formidable life to a very glossy Pinterest board. Hers was no Disney confection. She entered politics, endured the devastating loss of her husband and son, and even spent time behind bars during the Emergency. Beneath the silks and society photographs was a woman of considerable fortitude, whose most enduring accessories were perhaps kindness, resilience and an almost obstinate sense of hope. So, beyond the chiffon, here are some top-tier pearls of wisdom from a literal रानी 👑 (!!)

Ever flipped through the glossy pages of Vogue and briefly wondered if you’d accidentally picked up National Geographic? Not even a year old, and Vogue India already had people talking. People like The New York Times.

The August 2008 issue returned to one of fashion’s favourite forms of pornography: poverty. The shoot wasn’t the usual luxury-editorial impulse of putting a model in couture next to a crumbling wall in the name of “juxtaposition.” These were actual, unnamed people living in what the NYT described as “in-your-face poverty.” They were photographed by Jean-François Campos (the shoot used to be available on his website, not anymore IJBOL) on the busy streets alongside objects of almost comical luxury: a Burberry umbrella, a Fendi baby bib, a Birkin. You know, the essentials.

The idea was to democratise fashion, to suggest that beautiful objects and the fantasy of luxury needn’t belong exclusively to the people who could afford them. But when the prices of the handbags featured were more than what the “real” people could earn in a lifetime, well, one must ring the alarm on the moral fashion faux pas.

Tasteless? Tasteful? Tone-deaf? Perhaps all three, which is partly why we’re still talking about it. But you have to admit that there was certainly an editorial appetite then. That compulsion to provoke, delight, shock, whatever, but above all to remain memorable. Asked for her two cents amid the controversy, then EIC Priya Tanna said to let them eat cake and “Lighten up.”

Before ‘Naagin’ held every television screen captive, Nagraj was our venomous obsession. Introduced in 1986 by Raj Comics, he was a cast-away-prince-turned-killing-machine-turned-hero in tight purple briefs and knee high boots. With power like Vishfunkaar (venom breath that can melt metal) and command over a million snakes that resided in him (character development before AI 🤣), he was THE most powerful hero in desi comic history.

What Raj Comics did was turn Indian mythology and stories into a format that the youth were already consuming ferociously from foreign publications. They changed Western settings and brought in local perspectives. Like why should super-villains only attack America? 🙂‍↕️ The success was immense, with every kid saving up to buy the latest issue (they were not CHEAP!) or rushing to the nearest stores to rent them out. 

With readership declining, Nagraj has been largely forgotten. No major Bollywood adaptation has been made (although Ranveer was rumoured to take on the role?) and it unfortunately seems to not be anywhere in sight. But for the millennials and the 90s kids, the memories are still vibrant as the coloured pages of those comic strips. 

Since everyone wants to revive Indian crafts and story who is getting onboard for this revival?? Batao

The SoDelhi girls and the SoBo girls didn’t wear Juicy tracksuits they were basically born into them. You couldn’t separate girl from velour without some form of physical altercation. She lived in it, breathed in it, partied in it, went to the airport in it, flew private in it, probably cried outside Olives in it (someone call AD!). That tracksuit has seen marriages, divorces, affairs, scandals, friendship break-ups, suspiciously large natural diamonds and at least one family secret that absolutely cannot leave the WhatsApp group. The velour knows TOO MUCH.

Every few years a new generation discovers it and behaves as though they’ve unearthed Tutankhamun. When Balenciaga did their little juicy moment suddenly everyone wanted velour again. Now Tom’s Spidey has worn it and here we go again. Because that’s the thing about a Juicy tracksuit. It’s practically immortal. Trends come and go, marriages come and marriages definitely go, but JUICY remains.

Anyway, enough fashion history. I WANT THE GOSSIP. I want to hear from the SoDel and SOBO girlies who were actually THERE. What has your Juicy witnessed? Where did you wear it? Who did you kiss in it? Who did you divorce in it? What airport lounge has it slept in? What scandal did it survive? And when did you get your first one?

The tracksuit may have an NDA. You don’t. Tell me everything(!!)

In 2011, pre-influ, pre-Instagram and pre-Reels flattening everyone into the same-same algo-approved person, Burberry brought Art of the Trench to India. The premise was deceptively simple and actually rather brilliant: take one evergreen object, the classic Burberry trench, and document how personal style mutates across cultures, cities and people. High and low, dressed up, dressed down, skinny jeans, ballet flats, etc. The India chapter was photographed by @man0u, who left the relative sanity of his nine-to-five job and has spent nearly two decades travelling all over India documenting street style via @wearaboutblog, in collaboration with editor @dalchodha, who curated and styled not only India but several Art of the Trench projects globally. Looking at the pictures now feels almost anthropological. The poses, henny! The skinny jeans? The ballet flats lol! An ankle-length jean with a ballet flat was basically formalwear. People seemingly wearing clothes because they liked them rather than because 14 other people had received the same PR mailer that morning. An immaculate little time capsule of the 2010s and of a time when personal style was, rather quaintly, personal.

In life, there are bags and there are BAGS. There are those that hold your trash, a rogue lipstick, and receipts from God knows when, and then there are those that hold their value. No, not all bags are created equal, no matter what anyone says. Trust me. And in the feudal system of purses, the biggest faux (leather) pas is mistaking one for the other, especially when you’re about to “invest” a sizeable chunk of your salary in one.

Because a bag can be expensive without being valuable. It can be luxury without being an investment. It can also cost the GDP of a small island nation and still depreciate the minute it leaves the boutique. Such is capitalism sweetie!

Everyone can stop the WhatsApp-aunty-guessing game because the Bengal tiger is officially out of the bag, for the second time this year. On his current streak of dropping major news like casual administrative updates, Sabya has finally revealed what his collaboration with THEE MET actually is.

It’s a multi-year, almost Odyssean partnership (if you may) in which Sabya will study the museum’s vast collection and transform its cultural artefacts into exquisite modern-day objects of fashion. Jewellery, accessories, apparel, the works. Essentially, centuries of human civilisation, but make it Sabya.

For the first chapter, he’s releasing a line of high-end fine jewellery inspired by Byzantine objects in the museum’s collection, which will debut during his much-anticipated NYFW “don’t call it comeback” show

Just know the art connoisseurs with a pathological penchant for anything shiny, lavish and historically significant are going to go absolutely feral. Because what better way to intellectual-signal than having the biggest designer × biggest museum collaboration dangling around your neck? Nothing says “I understand Byzantine material culture” quite like wearing several lakhs of it to dinner lol 🤪

Sabya dropped a cryptic post at the ungodly red-eye hour, teasing a mysterious collab with the MET. Naturally, my mind has entered a state of speculative delirium. Could it be a blockbuster exhibition that leaves us collectively speechless? A colossal Bengal tiger installation prowling the hallowed museum halls? A return of his ICONIQUE headbands destined for the museum store shelves? Perhaps a desi sari-NoT-sari intervention at the MET Gala is in the works? Or, actually, is the museum playing host to his grand NYFW comeback show? 

The possibilities are becoming increasingly baroque. 

If even ONE of these predictions comes true, y’all owe me a trip to New York I don’t make the rules 🤣😬🫢☕️💅

The Falguni Shane bride is not about subtlety. She wants the shine, the shimmer, the feathers. She’s not shy. She works out, vacations in Menorca, and wants everyone to know she’s the centre of attention, and Fsp delivers it.

This time it’s about travelling to the most delectable destinations. The addition of the vivid embroidered scenes from the Taj to Paris to Bavaria, on the lehengas are for the girlies that have multiple country flags on their bios and stories of proposals by the Seine. 

Remember when Britney wore them back in the aughts? That wasn’t an accident. The brand has always occupied that unapologetically glamorous lane. In an industry obsessed with pivoting every other season, Falguni Shane has largely resisted the temptation to become somebody else.

With all the humdrum about craft revival and preservation, another designer brings another craft to the runway. Anamika teamed up with a group of women artists who practice the age-old tradition of Kalighat paintings and had them meticulously hand-paint her couture garments. The paintings, on organza and silk satin, became a part of voluminous ball gowns, sherwanis, and sheer slip dresses. As awe-inspiring as it all may be, after the show, Anamika shares with us one bitter truth about craft and artisans—they are not making any money. Even with all the social media optics and engagement farming, most artisans are still not making any money. 

The Kalighat paintings are iconic and lend a huge visual identity to Kolkata, yet the lack of patronage confused Anamika. “Craft is not something to be wrapped in muslin, framed, and put on the walls. It needs to be current and relevant. It needs to be in people’s lives.”, she said. For her, craft is not stagnant and needs experimentation. She believes in preservation but not freezing it in a bygone era. 

We asked her if there is a right way of using craft, and even she says there may never be a definite answer but to continue to engage. “As long as we engage with it, that’s the only way to survive.”
